title: Linear Changelog — Onyx Release Grid
description: A 2×2 developer-aesthetic bento that distills a software release into four equal tiles — New, Improved, Fixed, and API — each anchored by a status badge and a commit-style monospace tag on a near-black canvas. Where most bento templates flex layout variety, this one enforces strict parity to mirror the discipline of a real changelog.
philosophy: This template treats a release note as a contract, not a celebration. It borrows the visual grammar of Linear and Vercel: every tile earns its space with exactly one change, one badge, and one monospace tag — nothing more. It refuses decorative illustration, gradient washes, and expressive typography because the audience is engineers who distrust embellishment. The near-black ground and barely-lighter tile surfaces signal that the content is the UI, not a backdrop for it.
goodFor: Sprint retrospective release summaries presented to engineering teams
Product changelog slides inside developer-facing pitch decks
API version announcements to technical stakeholders
Internal release all-hands where four discrete update categories map cleanly to tiles
avoidFor: Consumer-facing marketing decks requiring warm, emotive, or illustrative visuals
Executive business reviews where non-technical audiences expect narrative flow
Presentations needing more than four distinct content blocks on a single slide
Brand storytelling slides where personality and texture must come through
author: harness

examples.promptCore: The slide reads like a terminal prompt at rest — near-black ground with almost no surface differentiation, the title the sole signal demanding attention. Mood references Linear release announcements and Vercel changelog headers: restrained, load-bearing, zero ornament. A single hairline rule is the only structural gesture, functioning as a visual commit separator rather than decoration. Avoid gradients, ambient glows, illustration, or anything that frames the content as a celebration rather than a precise, contractual declaration.

examples.layoutNotes: 12-column grid; a monospace release-version eyebrow tag is pinned to the upper-left in cols 1–2, acting as the slide's only header element. The main title occupies cols 2–10, vertically positioned in the upper third with a generous breathing margin below it. A full-width hairline rule bisects the canvas beneath the title, separating it from a sparse subtitle or release-date stamp in the lower zone. No footer band; a build-string or deck identifier sits flush bottom-right, outside the primary content columns.

examples.promptCore: The slide feels like a live developer-tool dashboard — austere, exact, and stripped of ornament. Four barely-elevated tile panels sit against a near-black canvas, distinguished from it only by a subtle tonal step, evoking a real changelog UI rather than a designed artefact. Composition is dense-modular and strictly symmetrical; every tile is a peer, never a hero, and the eye moves between them in equal beats. Avoid gradients, illustration, expressive curves, or any decorative mark that would soften the tool-native severity.

examples.layoutNotes: Four equal tiles fill a strict 2×2 grid spanning nearly the full canvas, separated by a thin uniform gutter with a narrow outer margin on all four sides. Each tile follows an identical internal scaffold: a status-badge pill anchored top-left, a single-line change description occupying the tile's mid-zone, and a commit-style monospace tag pinned to the bottom-left corner. Hierarchy is enforced entirely through weight contrast — badge label vs. description vs. tag — with no rule lines or decorative dividers between zones. A release version slug or slide index sits outside the grid boundary at the bottom-right of the canvas.
